I.	The theory of natural selection, as articulated by Charles Darwin and independently
formulated by Alfred Russel Wallace, is often celebrated not merely for its originality but for
its decisive explanatory economy. What distinguishes it from earlier speculative accounts of
life is its capacity to resolve, with remarkable conceptual restraint, the long-standing puzzle of
purposiveness in nature. Where earlier frameworks were compelled to invoke design or pre-
established harmony to account for the precise adaptation of organisms to their environments,
the principle of selection renders such assumptions not only unnecessary but intellectually
excessive.
Darwin’s insight did not emerge fully formed but was preceded by a careful engagement with
the problem of variability. Observing how human breeders selectively amplified desirable
traits, he recognised that transformation within species required no mysterious force, only the
consistent retention of certain variations over others. Yet the critical difficulty lay in
extending this logic to nature itself, where no conscious selector appeared to operate. It is here
that Darwin’s engagement with Malthus becomes pivotal: the realisation that organisms
reproduce in excess of what their environments can sustain introduces an unavoidable
condition of competition.
This condition, which Darwin termed the “struggle for existence,” is frequently misunderstood
when reduced to crude images of predation. Its true significance lies in the far subtler and
more pervasive competition among individuals of the same species, where even marginal
advantages determine survival. The evaluative force of Darwin’s argument rests precisely on
this point: what survives is not the strongest in any absolute sense, but the most suitably
constituted relative to specific conditions. In this sense, selection is less an event than a
continuous filtration.
Such a view compels a reconsideration of adaptation itself. Rather than being evidence of prior
intention, adaptation emerges as the cumulative outcome of innumerable eliminations, where
non-advantageous variations are quietly discarded. The elegance of this explanation lies in its
refusal to posit any guiding intelligence; instead, it locates order in repetition. Over successive
generations, this repeated selection produces structures that appear purposive, though they
are nothing more than the residue of what has endured.
It is this relentless emphasis on repetition—on the continual preservation of the relatively
better suited—that constitutes the true strength of the theory. By grounding complexity in a
simple, recurring process, Darwin not only displaces earlier metaphysical explanations but
also establishes a framework within which both diversity and precision can be understood
without recourse to external design. The enduring power of natural selection lies, therefore,
not in any single insight, but in the consistency with which it explains the emergence of form
through the repeated survival of the suitable.
Source: On Darwin’s Theory of Natural Selection — explanatory scientific text

Il.	It is tempting to judge comedy in rigid moral terms—either as harmless amusement or as a
form of insensitivity. However, such binary thinking fails to capture the inherently complex
nature of humour. Comedy should neither be dismissed as morally inferior nor accepted
without scrutiny; instead, it must be understood as a multifaceted human response shaped by
context, intention, and effect.
Critics of comedy, from Plato onwards, have often regarded laughter as a reflection of human
weakness, particularly when it targets the flaws of others. While this concern is not entirely
unfounded, it represents only a narrow interpretation of humour. The superiority theory
suggests that laughter arises from a sense of dominance, yet this does not exhaust the
possibilities of why people laugh. Alternative perspectives, such as the incongruity theory and
the relief theory, demonstrate that humour can emerge from cognitive surprise or
psychological release, rather than moral deficiency.
More importantly, the assumption that laughter directly reveals moral character is deeply
problematic. Individuals frequently laugh at situations without endorsing their underlying
implications, and to equate amusement with agreement is to misunderstand the nature of
human response. The moral evaluation of humour, therefore, cannot be detached from
situational context or individual sensibility. What appears offensive in one setting may serve
as coping or critique in another.
Beyond moral ambiguity, comedy performs essential social and psychological functions. It
fosters connection by creating shared experiences and strengthens bonds when individuals
laugh together. Simultaneously, humour provides a subtle means of challenging authority and
expressing dissent in environments where direct criticism may not be possible. In this sense,
comedy extends beyond entertainment to become a tool for negotiating social realities.
Given these considerations, it is neither reasonable nor productive to judge comedy through
rigid frameworks. Its significance lies in its flexibility—its ability to comfort, to critique, and to
connect. To reduce humour to a simple moral category is to overlook the very qualities that
make it meaningful within human life. Comedy must, therefore, be evaluated not in isolation,
but in relation to the contexts in which it operates.
Source: Adapted from “Is Comedy Good for Us?” by Damaris Stock, Philosophy Now

Il.	For as long as I could remember, my grandmother had been old. It was difficult to imagine

of prayers—seemed timeless, as though age had claimed her long before I came into the world.
In my childhood, we shared an intimate companionship. She would wake me in the morning,
prepare me for school, and accompany me to the temple where I studied. While I recited my
lessons, she remained absorbed in her scriptures. On our way back, she would feed stray dogs,
distributing pieces of bread with a sense of calm generosity. These routines created a rhythm
that bound us together.

Mickey Mouse!. The first Mickey Mouse cartoon actually completed was Plane Crazy. Inspired

inheritance, and live-in relationships across religious communities. Scheduled Tribes are exempted from
the law. The Code mandates compulsory registration of marriages and live-in relationships, prohibits

However, recent scientific research suggests that these natural cycles are now operating against a
backdrop of long-term human-induced warming. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Climate agencies have begun revising how such events are classified, as traditional temperature

XI.	In the law of torts, liability generally arises when a person causes harm to another through a
wrongful act or omission. However, not all damage results in legal responsibility. There are
situations where harm is caused without any human fault, purely due to natural forces beyond
control. In such cases, the law recognizes a defence known as the Act of God, also referred to as
Vis Major. This doctrine plays an important role in determining the limits of liability,
especially in cases involving natural disasters such as floods, earthquakes, storms, and
lightning. It reflects the principle that individuals should not be held responsible for events
that are entirely outside human foresight and control.
An Act of God refers to an extraordinary natural event caused exclusively by natural forces,
which is unpredictable, unforeseeable, and unavoidable despite reasonable care. The term Vis
Major is derived from Latin, meaning “superior force,” and both expressions are used

interchangeably in tort law. The essence of this defence is that when damage is caused solely
by natural forces, without any human intervention or negligence, the defendant cannot be held
liable.
For the defence of Act of God to succeed, certain essential conditions must be fulfilled. First,
the event must arise purely due to natural forces such as earthquakes, floods, cyclones, or
lightning, and if human involvement contributes to the damage, the defence fails. Secondly,
the event must be extraordinary and not something expected under ordinary circumstances,
which means predictable events like normal seasonal rainfall do not qualify. Thirdly, the event
must be unforeseeable so that a reasonable person could not have anticipated it through
ordinary knowledge or scientific means. Lastly, the event must be inevitable and unavoidable
despite the exercise of reasonable care and precautions.
A significant distinction exists between an Act of God and negligence. If damage is caused
entirely due to natural forces, liability does not arise. However, where a natural event
combines with human negligence, liability may still be imposed. For example, destruction
caused by an unprecedented flood may qualify as an Act of God, but if defective construction or
lack of maintenance contributed to the damage, the defendant may remain liable.
The doctrine also acts as an exception to the rule of strict liability. Under strict liability, a
person may be held liable even without negligence, but the defence of Act of God operates
where the harm is caused solely by natural forces that could neither be anticipated nor
controlled. Thus, even strict liability has limits when confronted with extraordinary natural
events. Courts have repeatedly emphasized that: (1) the natural event must be exceptional and
unprecedented; (2) there must be no human contribution to the damage; and (3) reasonable
care and precautions must have been exercised. If these conditions are not satisfied, the
defence is rejected.
The defence of Act of God is applied cautiously and is subject to several limitations. Firstly,
with advancements in science and technology, many natural events can now be predicted, and
therefore, if an event is foreseeable, the defence may not apply. Secondly, individuals and
authorities are expected to take reasonable precautions against known risks, and failure to do
so may result in liability. Thirdly, even minimal human negligence can defeat the defence
because the event must be entirely natural in origin. Lastly, modern courts have adopted
stricter standards due to improved disaster forecasting, better infrastructure planning, and
increased expectations of safety.
Although primarily a concept in tort law, Act of God is also relevant in contract law through
force majeure clauses. These clauses excuse parties from performing contractual obligations
when extraordinary natural events occur, although the extent of protection depends upon the
wording of the contract. The principle underlying this defence is reflected in the legal maxim
“Actus Dei nemini facit injuriam,” meaning that an act of God injures no one in the eyes of the
law. Ultimately, the doctrine of Act of God represents an important limitation on liability by

Genocide is a crime that involves acts committed with the intent to destroy a national, ethnic,
racial, or religious group. According to the United Nations, genocide requires a proven intent

The 1948 United Nations Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of
Genocide defines genocide as any act committed with the intent to destroy a group. This
definition does not include political groups or "cultural genocide".
The key elements of the crime of genocide, as outlined in Article II of the convention, include:
+ Acts: Genocide involves specific acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in
part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. The prohibited acts include killing
members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting
conditions leading to the group's physical destruction, imposing measures to prevent births
within the group, and forcibly transferring children from the group to another.

The perpetrator must have the specific intent to commit the acts mentioned above with the
purpose of annihilating the group. This distinguishes genocide from other crimes against
humanity.
